title: Roger Zelazny
dek_or_short_description: Science fiction writer and collaborator. Co-authored *Deus Irae* (1976) with PKD. Professional correspondence during 1972–1973.
body_markdown:
Roger Zelazny was one of the major SF writers of the 1970s, known for his lyrical prose and imaginative intensity. His correspondence with PKD documents a professional collaboration that would eventually yield *Deus Irae*, a novel born from their exchange about metaphysics, theology, and the nature of apocalypse.

*Deus Irae* — its title Latin for "God's Wrath" — was published in 1976 but was in development during the period of these letters. The novel dealt with religious experience and the possibility of salvation in a post-apocalyptic world, themes that aligned with PKD's theological obsessions after 2-3-74. Zelazny brought his own spiritual concerns and his mastery of narrative structure; PKD brought his metaphysical intensity and his conviction that high stakes were at stake.

What the letters suggest is a respectful professional relationship. Zelazny and PKD had compatible ambitions — both wanted SF to matter philosophically, not just as entertainment — and compatible temperaments. Their correspondence about *Deus Irae* would have been substantive, centered on plot, character, theology, and meaning.

The collaboration itself is an artifact of a particular moment in SF history, when major writers could undertake joint projects and when co-authorship was a path to deeper work, not a compromise. The novel that emerged was strange and ambitious, unclassifiable — neither wholly Zelazny nor wholly PKD, but a genuine synthesis.
summary: Roger Zelazny (1972–1973+), SF writer and collaborator on *Deus Irae* (1976). Professional correspondence about metaphysics, theology, apocalypse.
